Ares. The Olympian god of war, bloodlust, and violent chaos in Greek mythology. Unlike Athena, who represents strategic wisdom in combat, Ares embodies raw aggression, brutality, and the destructive aspects of warfare. He is portrayed as cowardly despite his strength, often bested by heroes and even by other gods, making him a figure of contempt as much as fear.

He was the son of Zeus and Hera, making him a full Olympian, yet despised by his own father for his viciousness and lack of martial wisdom. Ares represents the bloodlust, chaos, and slaughter of battle, the carnage and panic of warfare. This distinguishes him from Athena, who embodies tactical military strategy and righteous victory.

He appears repeatedly in the Iliad as both a fierce combatant and a buffoonish, whining figure who complains of wounds and runs from the battlefield when injured. He was famously wounded in combat by the mortal hero Diomedes, who was aided by Athena to pierce his divine body. This humiliation highlighted his inferiority to the war goddess herself.

He had a renowned affair with Aphrodite, goddess of love, that was discovered when her husband Hephaestus trapped them in a magic net. Their union produced fearful deities: Phobos, the embodiment of fear, and Deimos, panic itself. He is typically depicted as hot-tempered, brutal, aggressive, and rash, lacking the dignity, wisdom, and restraint valued by Greek culture. This made him a figure of ridicule despite his considerable power.

The Romans identified him with Mars, though notably Mars was treated with far greater respect as a symbol of disciplined military valor and civic duty rather than mere brutality. Sacred animals included the serpent and the vulture, while red, symbolizing blood, was closely associated with his violent and destructive nature. He shares a father with Zeus and stands opposed to Athena, the rival goddess of war. His forbidden divine lover Aphrodite bore him Phobos and Deimos. The mortal hero Diomedes wounded him with Athena's aid. His story appears prominently in the Iliad, the epic poem of the Trojan War. Hephaestus trapped and humiliated him by capturing him with Aphrodite in an unbreakable bronze net.
